Correct. Whoever reviewed and released it, and the organisation it went out on behalf of, answer for what it says.
Automation does not create a gap in accountability. Someone chose to deploy it and someone chose to send the output.
The prompt produced a draft. It was the review and the decision to send that made it the organisation's statement.

questions.q: An internal team wants to use Claude to screen job applicants. The correct response is:
opts: Proceed — it will save time
Flag it for legal and HR review first, since decisions about people carry specific fairness and regulatory obligations
Proceed if the prompt mentions fairness
Proceed but keep it undocumented
questions.exp: Decisions about people carry obligations most other tasks do not: anti-discrimination law, explainability requirements, and in some jurisdictions specific rules about automated decision-making in employment. That is a legal and HR question before it is a technical one, so it goes to the people who own it rather than being resolved by whoever is building the workflow. Note the answer is not necessarily no - reviewed, well-governed uses exist - but it is not a call for the implementing team to make alone. Mentioning fairness in a prompt does not create fairness, and keeping it undocumented removes the audit trail exactly where one is most likely to be demanded.
why: Proceeding on time savings alone skips obligations that attach specifically to employment decisions, which is where the legal exposure is.
Correct. Legal and HR review first, because decisions about people carry fairness and regulatory obligations that a project team cannot sign off alone.
A fairness instruction in the prompt is not a fairness control, and it would not satisfy any regulator or survive a challenge.
Keeping it undocumented removes the audit trail precisely where one is most likely to be required, which compounds the original risk.

questions.q: The most useful thing an organization can publish to keep AI use safe day to day is:
opts: A list of banned words
Clear guidance on what data may be used, what needs human review, and who to ask when unsure
A monthly usage leaderboard
A requirement that all output be rewritten by hand
questions.exp: The guidance people actually use answers the three questions that come up daily: what data may I use, what needs a human check, and who do I ask when I am unsure. Those turn a vague sense of caution into decisions someone can make at their desk, and the third is what keeps the first two from ossifying - there is a route for the cases the policy did not anticipate. Banned-word lists fail because they enumerate surface patterns rather than principles, a usage leaderboard measures activity rather than safety, and requiring everything to be rewritten by hand removes the benefit rather than managing the risk.
why: A word list enumerates surface patterns rather than principles, and it will not cover the situations people actually hit.
Correct. What data may be used, what needs human review, and who to ask when unsure - the three questions that come up daily.
A leaderboard measures activity. It says nothing about whether the use was appropriate, and it quietly rewards volume.
Mandatory manual rewriting removes the benefit instead of managing the risk, and tends to be ignored rather than followed.

questions.q: Claude is asked to produce content that would mislead customers about a product limitation. The right action is:
opts: Rephrase until Claude produces it
Decline — the problem is the request, not the tool's response to it
Produce it and add a disclaimer
Escalate to get approval to bypass the refusal
questions.exp: When a request is itself the problem, no phrasing fixes it. Content designed to mislead customers about a product limitation is wrong regardless of which tool produces it, so the right response is to decline and, if there is pressure behind it, raise it. That is the distinction worth internalising: a refusal on legitimate work is a context problem worth clarifying, but a refusal on a genuinely improper request is the system working, and treating it as an obstacle to route around means the person has become the failure mode. A disclaimer does not repair misleading content, and seeking approval to bypass the refusal asks someone to authorise the same thing.
why: Rephrasing until it complies pursues the same improper outcome. The problem is the content, not the wording that produced it.
Correct. Decline - the request is the problem, and no tool or phrasing makes misleading a customer acceptable.
A disclaimer attached to misleading content does not make it honest, and would not help if the claim were challenged.
Escalating for permission to bypass asks someone else to authorise the same improper outcome, which does not change what it is.

questions.q: Personal data appears in a document a colleague wants to process. The safest handling is:
opts: Process it and delete the output afterward
Remove or mask the personal data unless there is an approved basis to process it
Process only the first page
Rename the file
questions.exp: Personal data needs a lawful basis before it is processed, not a cleanup afterwards. Removing or masking it unless there is an approved basis keeps the task possible while removing the exposure, and it is usually straightforward - most tasks need the structure and content of a document rather than the identities in it. Deleting output afterwards does not help, because processing happened when the data was sent. Processing only part of a document reduces the volume without changing the question of permission, and renaming a file changes nothing about its contents at all.
why: The processing happens when the data is sent. Deleting the output afterwards does not undo it or make it permitted.
Correct. Remove or mask the personal data unless there is an approved basis, which usually keeps the task possible with the exposure gone.
Processing part of a document is still processing personal data. Reducing the volume does not address whether it was permitted.
A filename has no bearing on the contents. The personal data is in the document either way.

questions.q: Your customer asks where their data goes when they use Claude. The professional response is:
opts: Guess based on how similar tools work
Point them to the official documentation and terms for the specific deployment they are using, and involve the right specialist if unsure
Tell them it is completely private in every case
Say it does not matter for most companies
questions.exp: Data handling varies by deployment, plan and contract, so the honest answer points at the documentation and terms for the specific arrangement the customer is on, and brings in a specialist when the question goes beyond what you can source. Guessing from how similar tools behave is how commitments get made that the organisation cannot keep, and blanket assurances - it is completely private - are the specific failure to avoid, because they are unverifiable and will be tested. Saying it does not matter for most companies dismisses a question that is often a legal requirement for the person asking it.
why: Guessing from similar tools risks stating a commitment your organisation cannot honour, in writing, to a customer.
Correct. Point at the documentation and terms for their specific deployment, and bring in a specialist when it goes beyond what you can source.
A blanket privacy assurance is unverifiable and varies by deployment. It is the answer most likely to be tested and found wrong.
For many customers this is a regulatory requirement rather than a preference, and dismissing it damages the relationship and the answer.

questions.q: Claude's answer ignores half of a long instruction. The most effective fix is:
opts: Repeat the whole instruction twice
Restructure it — break the requirements into a numbered list and ask for each to be addressed
Write the instruction in capitals
Shorten the input document
questions.exp: Long prose instructions bury requirements. When half of one gets dropped, the fix is structural - break the requirements into a numbered list and ask for each to be addressed - because a list makes each item individually visible and gives you a way to check coverage afterwards. Repeating the whole instruction twice doubles the length without improving the structure, which usually makes the competition for attention worse. Capitals signal urgency without adding clarity and tend to skew the tone of everything around them. Shortening the source document addresses the wrong input entirely; the problem is in the instruction, not the material.
why: Repeating the whole thing doubles the length without improving structure, so the requirement that was already losing still loses.
Correct. A numbered list makes each requirement individually visible and gives you a way to verify coverage afterwards.
Capitals convey urgency rather than structure, and heavy emphasis tends to distort the tone of the surrounding response.
The document is not the problem. Shortening the source changes what is analysed rather than how the instruction is followed.

questions.q: Output quality degrades noticeably late in a very long conversation. The most likely explanation is:
opts: The model is tired
Early context has been crowded out as the conversation grew
Your network connection weakened
The subscription is throttled
questions.exp: Long conversations accumulate everything: superseded drafts, abandoned directions, resolved tangents. Earlier material that still matters ends up competing with all of it, so instructions become less prominent and quality drifts without any single moment of failure. That is the explanation the evidence fits - a gradual, cumulative decline. The alternatives all predict a different shape: fatigue would recover with rest, a network problem would show as errors or delays rather than subtly worse content, and throttling affects whether requests are served rather than how well they are answered. Matching the shape of the symptom to the shape of the cause is the troubleshooting skill here.
why: There is no fatigue and nothing that recovers with rest. The decline tracks conversation length rather than elapsed time.
Correct. Early context gets crowded out as the conversation grows, which produces exactly this gradual, cumulative decline.
A network problem shows up as errors, delays or truncation rather than as subtly less relevant content.
Throttling affects whether requests are served at all. You would see rejections or waits rather than a quality slide.

questions.q: The same prompt gives noticeably different answers on different runs. The best way to increase consistency is:
opts: Accept it as unavoidable
Tighten the prompt — specify format, constraints, and an example of the expected output
Send the request more slowly
Ask the question in a different language
questions.exp: Variation between runs is normal, and the lever you have is specification. Naming the format, the constraints and an example narrows the range of acceptable outputs, so the remaining variation happens inside a shape you defined rather than across the whole space. Accepting it as unavoidable gives up a control you have not used yet - most run-to-run variation traces to an underspecified request rather than to inherent randomness. Request timing has no effect whatever, and changing language introduces a much larger source of variation than the one you were trying to remove.
why: Much of this variation comes from an underspecified request rather than inherent randomness, so there is a control you have not used.
Correct. Specify format, constraints and an example, so the remaining variation happens inside a shape you defined.
Timing and pacing have no bearing on how a response is generated. Nothing about the request has changed.
Switching language introduces far more variation than it removes, and changes the output in ways you did not intend.

questions.q: Claude misunderstands a domain term that means something specific inside your company. The fix is:
opts: Avoid the term entirely
Define the term in the prompt the first time you use it
Use the term more often so it is learned
Ask Claude to guess the meaning
questions.exp: Internal jargon is genuinely unknowable from outside: a term that means something specific inside your company has a different common meaning or none at all, and the model will use the common one. Defining it the first time you use it is a one-line fix that resolves the whole conversation, and it is worth building into shared templates so it is not rediscovered each time. Avoiding the term forces circumlocution and loses precision. Using it more often reinforces nothing, since there is no learning between requests, and asking the model to guess invites a confident wrong reading that then propagates through everything downstream.
why: Avoiding the term costs you the precision it carries and forces awkward circumlocution around the concept you actually mean.
Correct. Define it on first use - a one-line fix that resolves the ambiguity for the rest of the conversation.
Repetition teaches nothing. There is no learning between requests, so the term is misread consistently rather than gradually understood.
Guessing produces a confident wrong interpretation that then propagates silently through everything built on it.

questions.q: A summary is accurate but written at the wrong level for its audience. The most direct fix is:
opts: Make it shorter
Name the audience and their expertise explicitly, and state what they need to do with it
Ask for 'a better summary'
Change model
questions.exp: A summary pitched at the wrong level is a specification failure rather than a quality one - the content is right and the framing is wrong. Naming the audience, their expertise, and what they need to do with the summary fixes all three dimensions at once: vocabulary, assumed background, and which details survive. That last part is what makes it work, since what a board member needs cut is exactly what an engineer needs kept. Making it shorter changes length without changing register, asking for something better restates the dissatisfaction without specifying the target, and changing model does not supply information you never gave.
why: Length and register are different problems. A shorter summary at the wrong level of expertise is still at the wrong level.
Correct. Name the audience, their expertise and what they need to do with it - that fixes vocabulary, assumed background and what survives.
Asking for something better restates the dissatisfaction without saying what would be right, so the next attempt is another guess.
A different model cannot infer an audience you never named. The information is missing from the request, not from the model.

questions.q: You suspect Claude has misread a source document you attached. The fastest way to confirm is:
opts: Re-attach the document and hope
Ask it to quote the exact passage it used before it continues
Ask whether it read the document
Rephrase the original question
questions.exp: Asking for the exact passage before it continues turns a suspicion into a check you can complete in seconds: either the quote is in the document and you can see how it was read, or it is not and you have found the problem directly. It also stops the error propagating into further work built on the same misreading. Re-attaching the file changes nothing about the interpretation. Asking whether it read the document invites a self-report generated the same way the original answer was. Rephrasing the question produces another answer without telling you whether the first one was grounded in the source at all.
why: Re-attaching does not change how the document was interpreted, and you still have no evidence either way.
Correct. A quoted passage is checkable in seconds, and a quote that is not in the document exposes the problem immediately.
A self-report is generated the same way the original answer was, so it produces reassurance rather than evidence.
A rephrased question yields another answer without telling you whether either one was grounded in the source.

questions.q: Claude produces a well-written answer that is confidently wrong. The most important lesson is:
opts: Fluency and accuracy are independent — polish is not evidence of correctness
The prompt was too short
The model needs replacing
Longer answers are more reliable
questions.exp: This is the single most important habit to build: fluency and accuracy are independent properties. The polish of an answer - its coherence, its confident tone, its specificity - is produced by the same process whether or not the content is right, so none of it carries information about correctness. That is why review has to be deliberate rather than instinctive, because the instinct being overridden is a reasonable one that works on human writing, where care usually does correlate with accuracy. Assuming prompt length or model choice explains a confidently wrong answer misses the general lesson in favour of a specific and usually incorrect diagnosis.
why: Correct. Polish is not evidence of correctness, which is why review must be deliberate rather than instinctive.
Prompt length may or may not be a factor here, and treating it as the lesson misses the general point about fluent output.
A well-written wrong answer is characteristic behaviour rather than a defect. Replacing the model does not remove the property.
Length correlates with neither accuracy nor reliability. A longer wrong answer is simply a longer wrong answer.

questions.q: A customer asks why Claude gave a different answer than their internal wiki. The most useful first check is:
opts: Whether the wiki is popular internally
Whether the wiki was actually supplied as a source, or whether Claude answered from general knowledge
Whether the question was phrased politely
Whether the wiki has images
questions.exp: Before investigating a discrepancy, establish whether the wiki was ever in play. If it was not supplied as a source, the model answered from general knowledge and the difference is expected rather than a defect - and the fix is to supply it, not to debug the answer. That check takes seconds and prevents a long investigation into a problem that does not exist. It also reframes the customer conversation usefully: the question becomes how to ground answers in their material, which is actionable, rather than why the model disagrees with them, which is not.
why: Internal popularity says nothing about whether the model had access to the document, which is the question that decides everything else.
Correct. Check whether the wiki was actually supplied as a source, since if it was not, a difference is expected rather than a defect.
Phrasing affects how a question is interpreted. It does not determine which sources the model had access to.
Images may affect how a document is processed, but that only matters once you know the document was supplied at all.

questions.q: A team needs to extract data from 100,000 scanned single-page invoices per month. Budget is constrained. Which model tier and strategy is optimal?
opts: Process all invoices with Claude Haiku 4.5 using structured JSON extraction prompts
Process all invoices with Claude Opus 5 with high temperature for maximum precision
Manually re-type all invoices to avoid AI token billing
Use Claude Sonnet 5 without any system prompt to minimize input tokens
why: Correct. Haiku suits high-volume, well-specified extraction, and structured JSON makes the output machine-usable and checkable.
This pairs the most expensive tier with a sampling parameter that current models reject outright, so it fails on both counts.
Manual re-typing trades a modest token cost for a large and ongoing labour cost, and introduces transcription errors.
Removing the system prompt saves a trivial number of input tokens while discarding the instructions that make extraction consistent.
questions.exp: Invoice extraction is high-volume, well-specified and structurally repetitive, which makes it the profile the fast tier serves best - and at 100,000 documents a month the per-item cost is the whole economics of the project. Asking for structured JSON output matters as much as the model choice: it makes the results machine-usable and checkable against a schema rather than needing to be parsed out of prose. Escalating to a more capable model is a reasonable response to measured accuracy problems on your own invoices, but it should follow evidence rather than precede it.

questions.q: Your team sends full-page diagram scans to Claude. What should drive how you size those images?
opts: Images are billed at a flat rate, so resolution does not matter
Higher resolution costs more tokens, so send the smallest size that keeps the detail readable
Always send maximum resolution, since token cost is unaffected by image size
Images are processed outside the token budget entirely
why: There is no flat image fee. Billing tracks the tokens the image resolves to, which depends on its dimensions.
Correct. Cost scales with resolution, so the size that just preserves the detail you need is the efficient choice.
The opposite of the truth, and an expensive assumption at volume, since resolution is the main driver of image cost.
Images are part of the input token budget like everything else in the request.
questions.exp: Images consume input tokens and the count scales with resolution. Current models support markedly higher resolution than earlier ones, which is why they read dense diagrams and screenshots so much better, but a full-resolution image can cost several times what the same picture cost on an older model. The practical rule is to send the smallest size at which the detail you need stays legible: downscale a photo of a whiteboard, keep a dense schematic sharp. If cost matters at volume, measure it with the token-counting endpoint on representative images rather than trusting a remembered formula.

questions.q: When prompting Claude to summarize medical research papers, which prompt structure best separates the source text from the task directives?
opts: Place instructions inside <instructions> and research text inside <document> tags
Put the research paper in ALL CAPS at the beginning of the prompt
Mix instructions throughout the document text in parentheses
Append 'Please do this accurately' at the very end with no tags
why: Correct. Tagged sections give an unambiguous boundary between source material and instructions, which helps both quality and safety.
Capitals convey emphasis rather than structure, degrade readability, and do nothing to separate the paper from the task.
Interleaving instructions creates precisely the ambiguity that delimiters exist to remove, and text in a document can then read as a command.
A politeness suffix adds no structure and no specification, so the model still has to infer where the source ends and the task begins.
questions.exp: Tagged sections give the model an unambiguous boundary between the material to analyse and the instructions to follow. That matters for quality, since instructions buried in a long document compete poorly with it, and it matters for safety: without a clear boundary, text inside a document can read as a command, which is the mechanism behind prompt injection. Putting the paper in capitals signals emphasis rather than structure and makes it harder to read. Scattering instructions through the text creates exactly the ambiguity tags remove, and a politeness suffix specifies nothing at all.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of using 'Role Prompting' (e.g., 'You are a Nobel-prize winning physicist') without providing reference materials?
opts: It styles tone and vocabulary but does not provide access to proprietary or ungrounded facts
It triggers an automatic API rate limit penalty
It causes the API to reject the request with HTTP 400
It forces the model into an infinite reasoning loop
why: Correct. It styles tone and vocabulary without granting access to proprietary or otherwise ungrounded facts.
There is no rate-limit penalty associated with framing. Roles are ordinary prompt text as far as the API is concerned.
A role is valid prompt content and does not cause a validation error of any kind.
Roles do not cause loops. The model responds normally, in the register the role implies.
questions.exp: Role prompting shapes how something is written - vocabulary, emphasis, which considerations get raised - and that is genuinely useful. What it does not do is supply knowledge. Telling the model it is a Nobel laureate does not give it access to your proprietary data or make an unsupported claim more reliable; it makes the same claim in a more authoritative register, which is arguably worse because it is harder to doubt. The practical rule is to use roles for framing and supply facts as facts. The distinction is worth holding firmly, because role prompting is often mistaken for an accuracy technique.

questions.q: An organization is deploying an internal customer support assistant that handles customer account inquiries. Which evaluation step is most critical prior to release?
opts: Testing against a representative benchmark of edge cases and adversarial prompt injections
Running the prompt once and verifying it looks polite
Ensuring the model temperature is set to 1.0
Checking that the prompt is fewer than 50 words
why: Correct. A representative benchmark including edge cases and adversarial prompts, which is where an untested assistant actually fails.
One polite-looking response tests the easy path, which was never the risk. It tells you nothing about hostile or confusing input.
This names a sampling parameter that current models reject, and sampling settings were never a substitute for evaluation anyway.
Prompt length is unrelated to whether the assistant behaves safely on difficult input.
questions.exp: Before a customer-facing assistant ships, test it on inputs that resemble what will actually arrive - including the awkward ones. A representative benchmark of edge cases and adversarial prompts tells you how it behaves when a customer is confused, hostile, or deliberately probing, which is precisely where an unevaluated assistant does damage. Adversarial testing matters specifically because the assistant handles account inquiries: anything untrusted arriving in its context is a potential injection vector. Checking a single polite response tells you about the easy path only, which is the path that was never going to be the problem.

questions.q: What is the role of a 'Golden Dataset' in prompt engineering evaluation?
opts: A curated set of representative input prompts paired with human-validated ideal outputs
A dataset containing only high-value financial transactions
A collection of prompts that always cost more than $1 to run
A marketing demo dataset that never fails
why: Correct. Representative inputs paired with human-validated ideal outputs, which is what makes prompt changes measurable rather than impressionistic.
The content domain is irrelevant. What makes a dataset golden is that its expected outputs have been validated by a person.
Cost is not a property of an evaluation set. Golden refers to the validation of the outputs, not to what the runs cost.
A set that never fails cannot discriminate between prompt versions, which is the entire purpose of holding one.
questions.exp: A golden dataset is the fixed reference that makes prompt changes measurable: representative inputs paired with outputs a human has confirmed are correct. Without one you are comparing new output against your impression of the old, which is not a measurement and quietly drifts. With one, you can tell whether a change helped, hurt, or traded one failure for another - and that last case is the one informal comparison always misses. The word golden refers to the outputs being human-validated rather than to any property of the inputs, which is why curation cost is the real investment.

questions.q: A customer asks how Anthropic decides what safeguards a frontier model needs. The accurate description is:
opts: Safeguards are fixed at launch and do not change
A published, tiered framework: as a model's capability crosses defined risk thresholds, stronger security and deployment safeguards are required
Safeguards are decided case by case with no published policy
Safeguards apply only to models offered through the API
why: The framework is designed to escalate as capability grows, which is the opposite of fixed at launch.
Correct. Tiered and threshold-driven, with stronger requirements as capability crosses defined levels.
There is a published framework. Saying otherwise understates what the organisation has committed to in public.
It is tied to model capability, not to the surface a model is served on.
questions.exp: Anthropic publishes a tiered responsible-scaling framework: capability is evaluated against defined thresholds, and crossing one triggers a stronger set of security and deployment requirements rather than a case-by-case judgement. Two things matter for an associate conversation. First, the framework is public, so point the customer at it rather than paraphrasing tiers from memory. Second, it is capability-triggered rather than product-triggered, so it is not a question of which surface a model ships on. For specific tier definitions and current commitments, cite the published policy; those details are updated over time.

questions.q: An enterprise customer requires that their confidential legal briefs processed by Claude are never retained on disk by Anthropic. Which mechanism provides this guarantee?
opts: An Enterprise Zero-Data-Retention (ZDR) agreement
Setting max_tokens=100
Adding 'CONFIDENTIAL DO NOT STORE' to the prompt text
Encoding the prompt in Base64 before sending
why: Correct. A Zero-Data-Retention agreement is the contractual mechanism that provides this guarantee.
That parameter caps output length. It has no relationship to retention, storage or contractual commitments.
Text in a prompt is content rather than contract. Writing an instruction into the payload creates no obligation on anyone.
Encoding changes the representation of the data, not what was transmitted or what either party agreed to.
questions.exp: When a customer's requirement is that content is not retained, the answer is a contractual arrangement rather than anything expressible in a request. A Zero-Data-Retention agreement is the enterprise mechanism that provides that guarantee, and it is negotiated rather than configured. This distinction matters because the alternatives look like technical controls and are not: parameters govern generation rather than storage, instructions in prompt text carry no contractual force whatever they say, and encoding the payload changes its representation without changing what was transmitted or who agreed to what.

questions.q: When Claude returns a safety refusal for a request to analyze a cybersecurity firewall log containing IP attack patterns, what is the best corrective action?
opts: Reframe the prompt to clearly state the defensive, authorized security auditing context inside <context> tags
Repeatedly retry the identical prompt with different punctuation
Pretend to be an attacker to trick the model into answering
Increase the temperature to 1.0 to bypass the classifier
why: Correct. State the defensive, authorised context explicitly in a delimited section, which is both the honest framing and the effective one.
Identical prompts with different punctuation resubmit the same ambiguity, so there is no reason for the outcome to change.
Adopting an attacker persona is deception rather than clarification, and it makes a legitimate task look like an illegitimate one.
Sampling parameters do not affect safety assessment and are rejected on current models regardless.
questions.exp: Defensive security work sits close to material that is genuinely restricted, so a refusal here is usually about missing context rather than the task itself. Stating the defensive, authorised purpose explicitly and in a clearly delimited section gives the assessment what it needs, and it is also simply the truthful description of the work. What separates this from the wrong answers is intent: clarifying is honest, whereas retrying with different punctuation is noise and adopting an attacker persona is deception. Sampling parameters are irrelevant, and current models reject them anyway - the framing of that option as bypassing a classifier is the giveaway.

questions.q: Why is human-in-the-loop (HITL) mandatory for high-stakes AI-generated regulatory compliance submissions?
opts: Because legal accountability remains solely with the submitting organization, and LLMs can hallucinate plausible errors
Because AI models refuse to write words longer than 10 letters without human approval
Because regulatory agencies automatically reject any document typed by an API
Because API tokens expire after 24 hours unless approved by a human
why: Correct. Accountability stays with the submitting organisation, and plausible-sounding errors are exactly what review exists to catch.
There is no such word-length behaviour, and nothing about human review is triggered by vocabulary.
Regulators assess content and compliance rather than how a document was typed. The concern is accuracy, not authorship mechanics.
Token expiry is an unrelated technical detail and has nothing to do with why review is required on a filing.
questions.exp: Human review is required on regulatory submissions because accountability cannot be delegated to a tool: the organisation signs the filing and answers for its contents. Combine that with the characteristic failure mode - fluent, specific, confidently wrong text - and the risk is a plausible error passing straight into a document a regulator relies on. Review is what catches it. The point is not that models are unusually error-prone here, but that this is a context where an error is both expensive and hard to retract, and where the reviewer is the accountable party regardless of what drafted the text.

questions.q: In Claude Projects, what is the optimal use of Project Custom Instructions?
opts: Defining organization-wide coding standards, output formats, and domain glossaries applied to all chats in the project
Storing individual temporary scratchpad notes that change every 5 minutes
Entering credit card numbers for billing automation
Writing a 50,000-word novel manuscript directly in the instructions box
why: Correct. Standards, formats and glossaries that should apply across every chat in the project, set once rather than re-pasted.
Rapidly changing notes belong in the conversation. Editing shared configuration for a transient scratchpad affects everyone using the project.
Payment credentials must never be placed in prompt or project configuration. This is a serious data-handling failure regardless of convenience.
A manuscript is content to work on rather than instruction about how to work, and instructions are not the place to store it.
questions.exp: Project instructions are the right home for anything that should apply to every conversation in that project: coding standards, output formats, domain glossaries, the conventions a team has agreed. Setting them once means every chat starts consistent without anyone re-pasting preamble, which is also what stops per-person drift. The test for what belongs there is stability - things that change every few minutes belong in the conversation, since editing shared configuration for a transient note affects everyone. Credentials never belong there under any circumstances, and a manuscript is content rather than instruction.

questions.q: How do Claude Artifacts enhance user experience when generating standalone code or UI components?
opts: They render code, SVG, and web apps in a dedicated interactive side-by-side pane without cluttering the chat history
They automatically deploy the code to AWS Lambda without user review
They encrypt the chat history with blockchain verification
They delete the code after 10 minutes to save disk space
why: Correct. Code, SVG and web apps render in a dedicated pane, so you can see the result without the chat filling with repeated copies.
Nothing is deployed anywhere. Publishing generated code without review would be a serious problem rather than a feature.
There is no blockchain involvement. This describes a rendering surface, not a storage or verification mechanism.
Content is not discarded on a timer, and a feature that deleted your work after ten minutes would be a defect rather than a benefit.
questions.exp: Artifacts give generated code, markup and small applications a dedicated pane to render in, separate from the conversation. The practical benefit is that you can see the thing working while the chat stays readable, and you can iterate on it without scrolling back through successive full copies of the same file. What it does not do is change deployment, security or persistence: nothing is published anywhere, nothing is encrypted differently, and the content is not discarded on a timer. It is a rendering and iteration surface, which is a smaller claim than the alternatives make and the accurate one.

questions.q: When designing an automated sentiment classification prompt, why is providing 3 few-shot examples superior to a 5-paragraph textual explanation?
opts: Examples demonstrate edge cases, label casing, and output syntax concretely, eliminating ambiguity
Few-shot examples bypass API billing charges
Examples allow the model to skip reading the system prompt
Examples increase model generation speed by 500%
why: Correct. Examples fix label vocabulary, casing, output shape and edge-case handling concretely, where prose leaves interpretive room.
Examples are input tokens like any other prompt content and are billed accordingly. There is no billing exemption.
Examples do not replace the system prompt. Both are read, and they work together rather than one bypassing the other.
Generation speed is unaffected by examples, and adding input tokens marginally increases processing rather than reducing it.
questions.exp: Examples specify by demonstration, which is why a few of them beat a long description. Three well-chosen sentiment examples fix the label vocabulary, the exact casing, the output shape, and how borderline cases are handled - all at once and unambiguously, where five paragraphs of prose leave room for interpretation that shows up as inconsistency. Choose them deliberately: examples are the strongest signal in a prompt, so the edge cases you include define the behaviour you get, and including only easy cases teaches the easy path. They cost input tokens like any other content, which is a real trade at volume.

questions.q: A developer wants Claude to format dates strictly as YYYY-MM-DD. Which prompt instruction is most resilient against format drift?
opts: Specify `<format>Date must strictly match regex ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$ (e.g. 2026-08-15)</format>` with 2 worked examples
Write 'Please give nice dates'
Add 'Do not use slashes' once at the top of the prompt
Ask the user to fix the dates manually afterwards
why: Correct. An exact pattern plus worked examples removes the interpretive room where format drift lives.
Nice is not a specification. It gives the model nothing to match and leaves every formatting decision open.
Ruling out slashes eliminates one wrong form and leaves every other one available, including dot and word-month variants.
Manual correction accepts the drift as permanent and pays for it on every run, rather than removing it once in the prompt.
questions.exp: The most resilient format instruction is unambiguous and demonstrated: an exact pattern the output must match, plus worked examples showing it satisfied. That combination removes the interpretive room where drift lives - a date can be written a dozen ways, and anything short of an exact specification leaves the choice open. Note this reduces drift rather than eliminating it, so a pipeline that depends on the format should still validate before use. The alternatives get progressively weaker: a single prohibition rules out one wrong form and leaves the rest, a vague adjective specifies nothing, and manual correction accepts the drift permanently.

questions.q: Why does Claude Haiku 4.5 respond faster than Claude Sonnet 5?
opts: Haiku skips safety evaluation to save time
It is built as the fast, lower-cost tier, trading speed and price against capability on hard tasks
Haiku servers are physically closer to every user
Sonnet deliberately delays responses to differentiate the tiers
why: Safety evaluation is not the variable being traded away, and telling a customer it is would be a serious misstatement.
Correct. A deliberate tier: faster and cheaper, with less headroom on genuinely hard reasoning.
Latency is dominated by generation rather than geography, and the tiers are served from the same infrastructure.
There is no artificial delay. The slower tier is slower because it is doing more work per token.
questions.exp: The tiers exist to give you a speed, cost, and capability choice, and Haiku sits at the fast end of it. Rely on published behaviour rather than reasoning from model internals, which Anthropic does not disclose: Haiku 4.5 is the fastest and cheapest tier, with a 200K context window and a 64K output ceiling against 1M and 128K on Opus 5 and Sonnet 5. The decision that follows is about the work rather than the architecture. Route high-volume, latency-sensitive, well-specified steps to Haiku, and keep genuinely difficult reasoning on a more capable tier.

questions.q: Why should prompt instructions be placed AFTER context documents in long-context prompts ('Lost in the Middle' mitigation)?
opts: Placing instructions at the very end ensures the model's attention is freshest on the required task when generation begins
The Anthropic API throws an error if documents are placed at the end
Instructions at the end cost 50% fewer tokens
Placing documents first makes the prompt cacheable
why: Correct. An instruction at the end sits closest to generation, which is where instruction-following is most reliable on long inputs.
There is no ordering requirement in the API. Both arrangements are valid requests; one simply works better.
Position within the prompt does not change token cost. The same content is billed the same either way.
Caching depends on a stable prefix rather than on document position, and putting documents first is compatible with caching.
questions.exp: On long inputs, the instruction placed last sits closest to where generation begins and is followed more reliably than the same instruction buried above thousands of tokens of source material. That is the practical half of the lost-in-the-middle finding: material at the extremes of a long context gets attended to more consistently than material in the interior. Pair it with clear delimiters around the document, which is the other half - the model needs to know where the source ends and the task begins, and without that boundary text inside the document can be read as instruction.

questions.q: What is 'LLM-as-a-Judge' evaluation methodology?
opts: Using a high-capability model (e.g. Claude Sonnet 5) with a strict grading rubric to evaluate outputs from another model or prompt version
Replacing legal judges in real courtrooms with AI algorithms
Running a prompt through an automated spell-checker
Asking 10 different people to vote on Twitter
why: Correct. A capable model applying a strict rubric to score another model's or prompt's output, which is what makes evaluation scale.
This describes replacing judicial decision-making, which is an entirely different claim and not what the technique refers to.
Spell-checking is mechanical text validation. A judge evaluates quality against criteria, which requires reasoning about content.
A public vote is unstructured opinion without a rubric, and is neither reproducible nor comparable between runs.
questions.exp: LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model with an explicit rubric to score outputs at a scale human review cannot reach - which is what makes systematic prompt comparison practical. The rubric is the load-bearing part: without concrete criteria the judge produces impressions rather than measurements, and those are not comparable across runs. Two limits are worth carrying. Judges inherit the biases of models, including a preference for whichever answer they see first, so serious comparisons swap positions. And they need calibrating against human judgement periodically, or you end up optimising confidently against a standard that has quietly drifted from the one you care about.

questions.q: Which of the following data types requires the highest scrutiny before passing into an external LLM prompt?
opts: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) such as Social Security Numbers and patient health records
Publicly accessible corporate marketing blog posts
Open-source software documentation
Standard dictionary definitions
why: Correct. Identifiers and health records carry the strictest statutory obligations and the highest penalties for mishandling.
Published marketing material is already public by intent, so sending it externally raises no confidentiality question.
Open-source documentation is published for public use and carries no confidentiality obligation.
Dictionary definitions are general reference material with no sensitivity or handling obligations of any kind.
questions.exp: Identifiers and health records carry the strictest handling obligations of anything on this list - specific statutory regimes, consent requirements, and real penalties for mishandling. They warrant the most scrutiny before leaving your systems, and often the answer is to remove or mask them rather than to find a way to send them, since most tasks need the structure of a record rather than the identity in it. The others are published or public material where the sensitivity question does not arise. Getting this ordering right is what stops a data-handling decision being made implicitly by whoever happens to be building the workflow.

questions.q: What is 'Prompt Injection' in LLM applications?
opts: An adversarial technique where untrusted input text overrides system instructions to hijack model behavior
A technique for making prompts run 10x faster
A database indexing optimization for vector databases
A method for adding vitamins to computer chips
why: Correct. Column relationships and headers stay explicit across rows, where the same data in prose becomes ambiguous quickly.
A table is ordinary text and counts toward the context limit exactly as any other content does.
Nothing is converted automatically. The model reads what you supply and does not transform values on its own.
Formatting has no relationship to batch processing or pricing. The discount comes from the endpoint used, not the content.
questions.exp: A Markdown table makes the relationship between a value and its column explicit, so the model can tell which figure belongs to which field across many rows. That structure survives where the same data as prose becomes ambiguous by the third or fourth row, and it is why tabular reference data is worth formatting deliberately rather than pasting. The benefit is comprehension only - a table is ordinary text that consumes tokens like any other, so it does not affect limits, cost or processing. Choose it because the model reads it more reliably, not because it changes anything about how the request is handled.

questions.q: What is the key advantage of using Markdown tables inside Claude prompt contexts for structured lookup data?
opts: Claude preserves column relationships and headers reliably across tabular rows
Markdown tables bypass the context window token limit
Tables automatically convert numbers into foreign currencies
Tables trigger free batch processing discounts
why: Correct. Reviewers can see intent and assumptions quickly, which is what makes reviewing generated code practical.
Comments are ignored at execution and have no effect on compilation or runtime speed in any language.
Security scanners analyse code rather than comments. Comments neither hide nor prevent any part of an audit.
Comments are output tokens like any other text, so they add slightly to cost rather than reducing it.
questions.exp: Comments alongside generated code let a reviewer see the intent and the assumptions, which is what makes review fast enough to actually happen. The important assumptions are the ones the code cannot state for itself - why this approach over the obvious alternative, what invariant the caller must hold, which edge case a branch exists for. Comments that narrate what the next line does add noise rather than help, so the instruction is worth phrasing as explain the reasoning rather than comment the code. None of this changes execution: comments are stripped or ignored at run time and affect neither speed nor security scanning.

questions.q: When generating code with Claude, why should you instruct the model to provide explanatory comments alongside the code?
opts: It allows developers to review the architectural intent and assumptions behind the implementation quickly
It forces the compiler to execute the code faster
It prevents the code from being audited by security scanners
It reduces the output token billing by 25%
why: Correct. A reviewer can see intent and assumptions quickly, which is what makes reviewing generated code practical at any volume.
Comments are ignored at execution in every language and have no effect on compilation or runtime speed.
Security scanners analyse code rather than comments. Comments neither conceal anything nor prevent any part of an audit.
Comments are output tokens like any other text, so they add marginally to cost rather than reducing it.
questions.exp: Comments alongside generated code let a reviewer see the intent and the assumptions, which is what makes review fast enough to actually happen. The assumptions worth stating are the ones the code cannot show for itself: why this approach rather than the obvious alternative, what the caller must guarantee, which edge case a branch exists for. Comments that narrate what the next line does add noise instead, so phrase the instruction as explain the reasoning rather than comment the code. None of this affects execution - comments are ignored at run time and do not influence speed or security scanning either way.

questions.q: An interactive autocomplete feature needs responses in well under a second. Which model fits best?
opts: Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Opus 5 with effort set to max
Claude Sonnet 5 with fifty few-shot examples
A multi-agent orchestrator that compares several drafts
why: Correct. Fast, cheap, and well matched to a high-volume task where each completion is individually low-stakes.
Raising effort deepens reasoning and lengthens the response, which is exactly the wrong trade against a sub-second budget.
Few-shot examples are input tokens on every request, adding both cost and latency at autocomplete volume.
Several models in sequence is the slowest option available, and autocomplete does not need cross-checking.
questions.exp: Autocomplete is the archetypal Haiku workload: high volume, latency-visible, and individually low-stakes. Every other option buys capability the task does not need and pays for it in time. Raising effort deepens reasoning, fifty few-shot examples inflate the input of every single request, and an orchestrator multiplies round trips. Note this is a fit judgement rather than a hard rule: if quality at Haiku proves inadequate you move up a tier and accept the latency, but the discipline is to start from the cheapest model that clears the bar and only escalate on evidence.

questions.q: Why is 'Negative Prompting' (e.g. 'Do not mention competitors, do not be rude, do not use jargon') often less effective than 'Positive Specification'?
opts: Positive specification provides an explicit pattern to follow, whereas negative lists leave an infinite space of alternate undesirable behaviors
The word 'not' causes an automatic syntax error in the API
Claude is unable to understand negative grammar
Negative words cost double the standard token rate
why: Correct. A positive specification supplies a pattern to follow, where a list of prohibitions leaves every unlisted alternative available.
Negation is ordinary language and causes no error. The issue is that it under-specifies rather than that it fails.
Negative instructions are understood. They simply constrain less than a positive specification of the same requirement.
Token pricing is uniform regardless of wording. Negation costs no more than any other phrasing.
questions.exp: A prohibition rules out one behaviour and leaves everything else open, so a list of things not to do still leaves the model choosing from an unbounded space of alternatives - including ones you would also reject but did not think to forbid. Describing what you do want closes that space: it supplies a target instead of a boundary. Prohibitions are not useless, and a few specific ones are worth keeping where a particular failure keeps recurring. But when a prompt is mostly a list of don'ts, the usual fix is to state the desired behaviour once, positively, and delete most of the list.

questions.q: When running automated prompt evaluations, what is 'Position Bias' in pairwise LLM comparison?
opts: The tendency of an LLM evaluator to prefer whichever candidate response is presented first (or second)
The physical geographic location of the evaluation server
The line number where the prompt was written in VS Code
The font size of the text on screen
why: Correct. A preference for whichever candidate appears first or second, regardless of quality, which quietly corrupts pairwise results.
Server geography has no influence on how an evaluator judges content. This is a property of the model, not the infrastructure.
Where a prompt sits in a source file is invisible to the evaluator, which sees only the content it is given.
Rendering and font are not part of what the evaluator receives. It reads text, not a visual presentation.
questions.exp: Position bias is the tendency of a model evaluator to favour whichever response it sees first or second, independent of quality. It matters because it silently corrupts pairwise comparison: if every run presents your new prompt second, a consistent positional preference reads as a consistent quality difference and you ship a change that did nothing. The standard mitigation is to run each pair in both orders and average, which costs twice as much and is worth it on any decision you intend to act on. It is a property of the evaluator rather than of the candidates being compared.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of deploying a public customer service chatbot without output moderation filters?
opts: Adversarial users may trick the bot into uttering offensive, brand-damaging, or legally binding incorrect statements
The bot will automatically delete the company's website
The bot will consume all available global internet bandwidth
The bot will refuse to talk to users who use mobile phones
why: Correct. Adversarial users can elicit offensive or brand-damaging content, or statements a customer can reasonably treat as binding.
A chatbot has no access to infrastructure. The risk is what it says, not what it can do to your systems.
Bandwidth is not a failure mode of a text assistant, and nothing about missing moderation affects network capacity.
Device type is irrelevant to moderation. This describes no behaviour the absence of output filtering would produce.
questions.exp: A public chatbot faces adversarial input by default, and without output controls the failure is reputational and sometimes legal: offensive content published under your brand, or a commitment - a refund, a guarantee, a price - that a customer can reasonably hold you to. Both are hard to retract once screenshotted. The reason moderation is the specific control is that prompt instructions alone are not a boundary; anything a user can write is untrusted input, and a determined user will find phrasing the system prompt did not anticipate. Treat the output path as the place to enforce what may leave.

questions.q: In high-reliability extraction pipelines, what is 'Schema Validation'?
opts: Parsing the LLM's JSON output against a strict JSON Schema (e.g. Zod / Pydantic) to catch missing keys or invalid types before saving
Asking the user if they like the color of the website
Compressing the JSON string with Gzip
Running a virus scan on the text file
why: Correct. Parsing against a strict schema catches missing keys and wrong types before the data reaches anything downstream.
This describes a user-experience question and has nothing to do with validating the structure of returned data.
Compression changes how data is stored or transmitted. It performs no checking of structure or content.
A virus scan looks for malicious files. It does not verify that a JSON payload matches an expected schema.
questions.exp: Schema validation checks the parsed output against an explicit definition - required keys present, types correct, values within allowed sets - before anything downstream consumes it. That is where the guarantee has to live, because instruction alone is a request rather than a contract: the first malformed response reaches your database unless something is checking. The distinction worth holding is between structurally valid and correct. Validation catches a missing field or a string where a number belongs; it cannot catch a plausible value that happens to be wrong, which is why it complements review rather than replacing it.

questions.q: You need Claude to return JSON that always matches your schema. The most reliable approach is:
opts: Ask it to write reasoning in thinking tags before the JSON
Constrain the response with a schema, and validate what comes back before you use it
Instruct it to output only JSON and parse whatever arrives
Ask for JSON twice and use whichever response parses
why: A dated pattern. Current models reason without being asked, and reasoning inside the payload is exactly what breaks strict output.
Correct. Constrain the shape at the request level, then validate before use, so the guarantee lives in code.
An instruction is a request, not a guarantee. Without validation the first malformed response reaches your database.
Retrying until something parses hides the failure rather than fixing it, and doubles cost on every bad response.
questions.exp: Two layers do the work here and neither of them is a prompt phrase. Constrain the output shape at the request level so the model generates against your schema rather than being asked nicely for it, then validate the parsed result before it reaches anything downstream. The guarantee you want is enforced by your code, not by wording. The scratchpad pattern was a genuine technique on models that did not reason by default; current models think adaptively without being told to, and asking for reasoning inside the response fights the structured output rather than helping it.

questions.q: When designing prompts for multi-lingual translation, what instruction prevents the model from adding unnecessary conversational filler (e.g., 'Here is your translation:')?
opts: Instruct: 'Output ONLY the direct translation inside <translation> tags with no preamble, explanations, or commentary.'
Write 'Please translate politely'
Set temperature to 1.0
Send the prompt 3 times in a loop
why: Correct. State the output contract explicitly and delimit it, so extraction stays reliable even if a stray sentence appears.
Politeness shapes register rather than structure, and does nothing about preamble appearing before the content you want.
Sampling settings do not govern output structure, and current models reject them regardless.
Repeating the request produces several responses each with their own preamble, which multiplies the problem rather than solving it.
questions.exp: Conversational preamble appears because the model is being helpful in a chat register, and the fix is to state the output contract explicitly: only the translation, inside delimiters, with no commentary. The delimiters do the real work in a pipeline, because they give you something unambiguous to extract even if a stray sentence does slip through - which turns a formatting problem into a parsing step rather than a failure. Politeness instructions do not address structure at all, sampling settings are unrelated and rejected on current models anyway, and repeating the request produces three responses with three preambles.

questions.q: Which Claude model is the balanced default for enterprise coding, complex analysis, and multi-step reasoning?
opts: Claude Sonnet 5
Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Opus 5 for every task regardless of difficulty
Whichever model was released most recently
why: Correct. The balanced default, strong on coding and analysis without Opus pricing.
The fast, low-cost tier. Right for high-volume simple work, not the default for complex analysis.
Opus 5 earns its cost on hard reasoning and high-stakes work; applying it everywhere pays a premium on tasks that never needed it.
Release date says nothing about fit. Choose on the difficulty of the task and the cost of being wrong.
questions.exp: Sonnet 5 is the balance point: near-Opus quality on coding and agentic work at Sonnet pricing, with the same 1M context window and 128K output ceiling. Haiku 4.5 is the fast, cheap tier for high-volume simple work and carries tighter limits at 200K context and 64K output. Opus 5 earns its cost when the reasoning is genuinely hard or a wrong answer is expensive, but defaulting everything to it is how spend climbs without a matching gain in quality. Recency is not a selection criterion at all: the newest model is not automatically the best fit for a given task.

questions.q: When summarizing multiple conflicting customer reviews, what prompting strategy yields the most balanced synthesis?
opts: Instruct Claude to categorize feedback into separate <positive_themes> and <critical_themes> with citing quote snippets before summarizing
Instruct Claude to only read the 5-star reviews
Ask Claude to pick whichever customer sounds friendliest
Tell Claude to invent 10 additional happy customer reviews
why: Correct. Categorised themes with supporting quotes force balanced coverage and anchor every claim to text you can verify.
Reading only five-star reviews selects for the conclusion in advance, which produces a summary of your filter rather than of the feedback.
Tone is not a proxy for representativeness. The friendliest reviewer is not the most typical one.
Inventing reviews fabricates evidence. This would misrepresent customer feedback entirely, regardless of how the summary reads.
questions.exp: Asking for categorised themes with supporting quotes does two things at once. It forces coverage of both sides, so a synthesis cannot quietly weight toward whichever reviews were more numerous or more emphatic; and it makes the summary checkable, because each theme is anchored to text you can go and read. That combination is what turns a plausible-sounding synthesis into one you can defend. Note it does not resolve the disagreement for you - conflicting reviews often reflect genuinely different experiences, and a summary that surfaces the conflict clearly is usually more useful than one that smooths it into a single verdict.

cards.f: What CCAO-F study domains does this app use?
cards.b: Prompting · Output Evaluation · Model Selection · Workflow Integration · Knowledge Management · Governance & Risk · Troubleshooting. These are **this app's** groupings, not published exam weightings — the official blueprint lives in Anthropic Partner Academy. Treat them as a study structure, and verify anything you plan to rely on against the official guide.

cards.f: What does CCAO-F cost?
cards.b: $99 USD, confirmed on Anthropic's public Pearson VUE listing. Format figures such as question count and time limit are reported by third-party study sites rather than by Anthropic, so treat them as indicative and check the official exam guide. Domain weightings have no public corroboration at all and are not stated here.

cards.f: Hallucination
cards.b: Fluent, confident output containing fabricated or unsupported claims. The danger is that the surface cues people use to judge reliability — coherence, specificity, an assured tone — are produced identically whether or not the content is true. Mitigate by grounding in supplied sources, asking for quoted passages, and verifying anything a reader will act on.

cards.f: When should a human stay in the loop?
cards.b: Wherever accountability sits: binding commitments, decisions about people, regulatory filings, and anything leaving the organisation. The test is who answers for the outcome, not how difficult the task is. Note the boundary is the *decision* — drafting, summarising and analysing can all be assisted right up to the point of commitment.

cards.f: Projects (Claude feature)
cards.b: Persistent workspaces holding custom instructions and knowledge files, so recurring work starts from the same grounding without anyone re-pasting context. The main risk to manage is staleness: a superseded document produces confidently outdated answers, and nothing in the output signals it. Curation is the ongoing cost, not a one-off setup step.

cards.f: Role prompting
cards.b: Assigning a persona to shape tone, perspective and domain conventions. It genuinely changes emphasis and vocabulary — and it grants no knowledge. A role cannot supply your proprietary data or make an unsupported claim more reliable; it states the same claim in a more authoritative register, which is arguably worse. Use roles for framing, and supply facts as facts.

cards.f: Few-shot prompting
cards.b: Including worked examples of input and desired output so the model matches the pattern. Examples are the strongest signal in a prompt: they fix structure, depth, formatting and edge-case handling at once, unambiguously. Choose them deliberately — the model matches their length and register too, and a set showing only easy cases teaches the easy path.

cards.f: Haiku vs Sonnet vs Opus — quick rule
cards.b: Haiku 4.5: fast and cheap for high-volume, well-specified work; 200K context, 64K output. Sonnet 5: the balanced default for most substantive work; 1M context, 128K output. Opus 5: hardest reasoning and highest-stakes judgement, same limits. Start at the cheapest tier clearing your quality bar and escalate on measured evidence, not on caution.

cards.f: Web search vs training data
cards.b: Training data has a cutoff, so current or private information is not available to be recalled — the model is not reasoning badly, it simply never had the fact. Search fetches at request time and closes that gap. A larger context window lets you supply more yourself but retrieves nothing, and deeper reasoning adds no facts.

cards.f: Fix for degraded answers in a long chat
cards.b: Accumulated context has crowded out what matters — superseded drafts, abandoned directions, resolved tangents all compete with the instructions still in force. Start a fresh conversation seeded with a deliberate summary of current requirements, decisions made and open questions. The curation is most of the value; a long conversation is not the same as a well-informed one.

cards.f: Data governance first question
cards.b: Is this data class approved by policy for this tool? It comes first because it can make the whole task impermissible, and no amount of prompt quality rescues data you were not permitted to send. When the answer is no, the useful help is a permitted route — masked data, an approved deployment, a different process — rather than a better prompt.

cards.f: Making outputs verifiable
cards.b: Ask for the specific source passage behind each claim. That converts verification from judging whether something sounds right — exactly the judgement fluent writing defeats — into comparing a quote against a document, which is fast and mechanical. A quote that is not in the source exposes the problem without evaluating the argument at all.

cards.f: What is the token cost formula for images and PDF pages processed by Claude?
cards.b: Images consume input tokens, and the count scales with resolution. Current models read images at markedly higher resolution than earlier ones, which is why they handle dense diagrams well — and a full-resolution image can cost several times what the same picture cost before. Send the smallest size that keeps the detail legible, and measure with the token-counting endpoint rather than trusting a remembered formula.

cards.f: What are Anthropic AI Safety Levels (ASL-1 to ASL-4)?
cards.b: Anthropic's published responsible-scaling framework: capability is assessed against defined thresholds, and crossing one triggers stronger security and deployment requirements. Two properties matter in a customer conversation — it is capability-triggered rather than product-triggered, and it is public, so cite the published policy rather than paraphrasing tier definitions from memory, since those are updated over time.

cards.f: When should Temperature be set to 0.0?
cards.b: It should not be. Sampling parameters — temperature, top_p, top_k — are removed on current models: Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and 4.7 reject them outright and Sonnet 5 rejects non-default values. Steer behaviour with prompting and structured outputs instead. Worth knowing that temperature 0 never guaranteed identical output even where it was accepted; it narrowed sampling, which is not determinism.

cards.f: What is an Enterprise Zero-Data-Retention (ZDR) agreement?
cards.b: A contractual commitment that prompt inputs and completions are not retained on persistent storage or used for training. The important property is that it is contractual — negotiated rather than configured, so no parameter, header or instruction in a prompt achieves it. When a customer with regulatory obligations asks, point them at the agreement for their deployment.

cards.f: Why are XML tags preferred over markdown headers for prompt sectioning?
cards.b: Tags give an unambiguous boundary between source material and instructions, and models are trained to respect that structure. It matters for quality, since instructions buried in a long document compete poorly with it — and for safety, because without a boundary text inside a document can read as a command. That is the mechanism behind prompt injection.

cards.f: What is the primary benefit of few-shot prompting?
cards.b: It teaches structure, formatting and edge-case handling by demonstration rather than description, which removes the interpretive room where inconsistency lives. One filled-in example fixes section order, depth and tone at once. The trade-off is that examples cost input tokens on every request, and a poorly chosen one anchors the output to its length and style.

cards.f: How does Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting reduce reasoning errors?
cards.b: It was a real technique on models that did not reason by default, and on current models it is not how reasoning is controlled. Depth is a property of the request — adaptive thinking, with an effort level setting how deep it goes. A prompt phrase changes the wording of the answer rather than whether the model reasons.

cards.f: What is the only valid way to verify LLM factual claims for external publication?
cards.b: Independent verification against primary sources. Asking the model whether it is sure produces a self-assessment generated by the same process that produced the claim, so a confident retraction and a confident confirmation cost exactly the same. Running the prompt twice measures consistency rather than correctness — two wrong answers can agree perfectly.

cards.f: What is the valid criterion for escalating from Haiku to Sonnet or Opus?
cards.b: Observed reasoning or comprehension failures on your own evaluation cases. That is direct evidence capability is the binding constraint. The common false signals are prompt length, which is a context-window question, and stakeholder seniority, which raises the cost of being wrong without making the task harder — it may justify more review rather than a bigger model.

cards.f: Where should persistent project-wide conventions and schemas be placed in Claude Projects?
cards.b: In the project's custom instructions, so they apply to every conversation without anyone re-pasting them, and a change goes through one place rather than many. The test for what belongs there is stability: anything changing every few minutes belongs in the conversation instead. Credentials never belong there under any circumstances.

cards.f: What is the appropriate response when Claude refuses a query on safety grounds?
cards.b: Supply the legitimate context the assessment is missing — what the work is, why it is authorised, what the output is for — and escalate through proper channels if it still declines. Note the distinction: clarifying intent is honest, whereas rephrasing to conceal it is a different act even when the words look similar. A refusal on a genuinely improper request is the system working.

cards.f: What is the best way to ensure Claude outputs valid, parseable JSON?
cards.b: Constrain the output shape at the request level with a schema, then validate the parsed result before anything downstream consumes it. Asking nicely produces valid JSON most of the time, which is the worst failure profile available — reliable enough to pass testing and frequent enough to break in production. The guarantee has to live in your code.

cards.f: What is the rough rule of thumb for English word-to-token conversion?
cards.b: Roughly 0.75 words per token for English, so 100 words is about 130 tokens. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude sanity check only: the real count is model-specific and comes from the token-counting endpoint. Other providers' tokenizers undercount Claude noticeably, and the gap widens on code and non-English text.

Welcome — this lesson assumes zero prior knowledge. By the end you'll have the vocabulary and mental model you need before any of the exam domains will make sense.

What is Claude?

Claude is a large language model (LLM) made by Anthropic — a computer program trained on enormous amounts of text that learned to predict, very well, what text should come next given some input. When you type a message, Claude reads it and generates a response one small chunk of text at a time. It doesn't 'look things up' the way a search engine does by default — it generates each response fresh, based on patterns learned during training, unless it's specifically given a tool like web search.

That single fact — Claude generates plausible text rather than retrieving verified facts — is the root of almost everything in the Output Evaluation domain later in this guide. Keep it in mind.

A conversation is just this loop, repeated — nothing more mysterious than that.

A short glossary you'll see everywhere

  • Prompt: the text you send Claude — your question, instruction, or request
  • Token: a chunk of text (roughly ¾ of a word on average) that Claude reads and generates in. Costs and limits are usually measured in tokens, not words or characters
  • Context window: the total amount of text (your messages, any documents, and Claude's replies) that Claude can 'see' at once, measured in tokens. Once a conversation exceeds it, the oldest content starts falling out of view
  • Model: a specific version of Claude (e.g. a fast one, a balanced one, a top-capability one) — see the Model Selection lesson
  • System prompt: background instructions set once (often by whoever built the tool you're using) that shape how Claude behaves for the whole conversation, separate from what you type
  • Hallucination: when Claude states something fabricated or wrong with the same fluent confidence as something true — this is the single most important risk to understand before using any LLM for real work
  • Project: a persistent workspace in Claude with its own instructions and reference documents, so you don't retype context every conversation

Why certification, and why this one first?

Anthropic's four certifications build on each other: Associate (this one) is for anyone using Claude as a daily work tool — no coding required. Developer is for engineers integrating Claude via API and code. Architect Foundations and Architect Professional are for people designing multi-step, tool-using agentic systems. If you're new to all of this, mastering the seven domains ahead — Prompting, Output Evaluation, Model Selection, Workflow Integration, Knowledge Management, Governance & Risk, and Troubleshooting — is the right on-ramp before touching the more technical certs.

Deep Dive: How Tokenization Works in Practice

Models do not read words or letters — they read token IDs. A token is a string of characters mapped to an integer in a lookup vocabulary (~100,000 unique tokens). Common English words like "apple" are a single token, whereas rare terms, technical code identifiers like "getUserAuthToken", or complex foreign language words are split into multiple sub-word tokens.

Context assembly pipeline: Stable system prefix → Dynamic history & retrieved context → Token generation loop.

Token Count Rule of Thumb

  • 100 English words ≈ 130 tokens.
  • 1KB of JSON code ≈ 250 to 350 tokens (punctuation and syntax increase token density).
  • Always calculate costs and context bounds using token counts, not character or word counts.
Real-World Case Study — Prompt Token Density

Problem: A team uploaded a 50-page raw uncompressed JSON dump (120,000 tokens) into every prompt turn for a simple daily query.

Architectural Decision: They extracted key key-value pairs into plain text tables, reducing token consumption by 65% while keeping model recall accuracy at 100%.
